claims.text: A combined DFT, machine-learning, Boltzmann-transport, and Green–Kubo approach can predict the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than earlier analytical approaches.
The proposed approach can isolate the phonon thermal-conductivity contribution from the electronic contribution.
The target material is high-purity, single-phase, defect-minimal bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine-learning adjustments to DFT outputs can produce realistic anharmonic interatomic potentials for HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed method is applicable to defect-free or minimally contaminated HfNbTaTiZr from 200 to 1200 K.
Machine-learning corrections can make the interatomic force constants account for anharmonic effects and local lattice distortions.
DFT supplies baseline phonon spectra and interatomic force constants.
Machine learning refines the DFT description to capture atomic-scale anharmonicity and fluctuations.
Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo calculations using the refined force description simulate lattice heat flow.
Focusing only on phonon properties prevents conflation of lattice and electronic heat transport.
The proposed method will reduce lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction error by as much as approximately 30% relative to conventional Debye-based or analytical estimates.
Low-temperature measurements indirectly indicate comparable lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Previous Debye-based and analytical approaches yield total thermal-conductivity estimates of 10–17 W/(K·m) for HfNbTaTiZr samples containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Previous approaches do not separately capture lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Below 200 K, separating lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions is more difficult.
Electron–phonon interactions may be more strongly coupled below 200 K.
The estimated 30% improvement is based on earlier comparative studies rather than direct measurement.
Independent electrical or Hall measurements can be used to estimate the electronic contribution and thereby isolate the lattice contribution.
A persistent deviation greater than ±30% between measured and predicted lattice thermal conductivity would falsify the accuracy hypothesis.
